subject: science
skillName: Matter Is Made of Tiny Particles
intro: All matter is made of particles that are far too small to see, even with a regular microscope. A model, such as drawing tiny dots or circles, helps us picture these particles. The particle model explains many things we observe: a gas spreads out to fill its whole container because its particles move freely and far apart, a smell travels across a room because particles leave the source and spread through the air, and air takes up space and has weight even though we cannot see it. In solids the particles are packed closely, in liquids they are close but can slide past each other, and in gases they are spread far apart.

items.prompt: A student opens a bottle of perfume at the front of a classroom. A few minutes later, students at the back can smell it. Use the particle model to explain why.

steps: All matter, including perfume and air, is made of tiny particles that are too small to see.
Perfume particles leave the open bottle and spread out, moving in all directions through the air.
Over a few minutes the particles travel far enough to reach the back of the room, where students smell them.
solution.answer: Tiny perfume particles spread out through the air until they reach the students at the back.

items.prompt: A sealed, empty-looking plastic bottle is squeezed. It feels firm and springs back. What does this tell you about what is inside, using the particle model?

steps: The bottle is not truly empty; it is filled with air.
Air is matter made of tiny particles that take up space.
When you squeeze the bottle the air particles are pushed closer and resist, so the bottle feels firm and springs back.
solution.answer: The bottle is full of air particles that take up space, so it resists being squeezed.

items.prompt: A student draws a model of a solid, a liquid, and a gas using small circles for particles. How should the circles be arranged in each one?

steps: In a solid the particles are packed tightly together in a fixed pattern, so draw circles close together and neat.
In a liquid the particles are still close but not in a fixed pattern, so draw circles close but able to slide past one another.
In a gas the particles are spread far apart and move freely, so draw circles with large spaces between them.
solution.answer: Solid: circles packed tightly. Liquid: circles close but loose. Gas: circles spread far apart.

items.prompt: Why can we not see the individual particles that make up a drop of water?

steps: The particles that make up matter are extremely small.
They are far too small to be seen with our eyes or even with a classroom microscope.
solution.answer: Because the particles are far too small to be seen, even with a microscope.

items.prompt: A balloon is blown up with air. Use the particle model to explain why the balloon gets bigger.

steps: Air is made of tiny particles that take up space.
Blowing adds more air particles inside the balloon.
The added particles push out on the balloon walls, so the balloon expands.
solution.answer: More air particles are added inside, and they take up space and push the balloon walls outward.

items.prompt: A sugar cube is stirred into a glass of water and seems to disappear, but the water tastes sweet. Use the particle model to explain where the sugar went.

steps: The sugar is made of tiny particles.
Stirring separates the sugar particles and spreads them out among the water particles, where they are too small to see.
The sugar is still there, which is why the water tastes sweet.
solution.answer: The sugar particles spread out among the water particles and are too small to see, so the water tastes sweet.
